We show that polynomials with essentially nonpositive coefficients belong to this class and establish a composition principle that yields further examples, including componentwise univariate compositions and compositions with structured quadratic maps motivated by source-localization loss functions. We then derive theorems of the alternative that provide SOS certificates for infeasibility of systems of strict inequalities involving Jensen-type polynomials and universally quantified variables. We illustrate our results through two applications, with numerical examples. First, we show that source-localization problems admit an exact SOS reformulation under a simple dimension condition, and that an optimal solution can be recovered by solving a semidefinite program (SDP) and applying the explicit Jensen map. Second, our SOS certificates yield two {\it convergent} SDP hierarchies for semi-infinite optimization with Jensen-type polynomials, providing upper and lower bounds on the optimal value. We also establish finite-convergence and solution-extraction results, under flat truncation rank condition and the associated Jensen maps.
☆ Statistical robustness and time consistency in risk averse optimization
Alexander Shapiro, Yan Li
The aim of this manuscript is to investigate risk measures which are not necessarily convex. We show that law invariant coherent risk measures are not robust with respect to contamination of the probability measure, in the sense that an arbitrarily small contamination can change their values by an arbitrary amount. This contrasts with the Value-at-Risk, which is robust against such contamination. In addition, we show that for a given law invariant risk measure and a given policy, one can construct, under mild conditions, conditional risk measures with respect to which this policy is time consistent, in the frameworks of both Markov Decision Processes and Stochastic Optimal Control.

Custom GPU kernels implemented with Triton reduce the launch and memory overhead of their sequential evaluation. With the smallest open instance having as few as 512 binary decision variables, the proposed IPs offer a challenging and intriguing combinatorial problem. In addition, we extend the problem to higher-dimensional grid graphs and provide solutions for unexplored and unsolved instances.

☆ Small-Gain Analysis of Robust Event-Triggered Extremum Seeking for Scalar Maps
Victor Hugo Pereira Rodrigues, Tiago Roux Oliveira, Miroslav Krstic, Zhong-Ping Jiang
We study a sample-and-hold implementation of gradient extremum seeking for a scalar quadratic map in which the control signal is refreshed only when an event occurs. The event generator acts on the demodulated gradient signal as it is actually measured, rather than on its averaged version, and contains a strictly positive offset, following the small-gain philosophy for robust event-triggered control. Rather than invoking averaging theorems, we work directly with the exact dynamics of the parameter estimation error. In the scalar setting, the demodulated gradient has an explicit sinusoidal structure, which is exploited through a change of variables that absorbs the zero-mean oscillatory perturbation, together with a quadratic Lyapunov function and the persistence of excitation of the probing signal. For a sufficiently fast dither, the estimation error is shown to decay exponentially to a residual neighborhood of the origin whose size is quantified by the dither amplitude and frequency, and by the relative threshold and the offset of the event generator. All constants, including the input-to-state stability gain of the extremum seeking loop, the admissible dither frequency and the positive lower bound on the time between two consecutive events, are given in closed form, so that Zeno behavior is excluded. A simulation example illustrates the results.

☆ An α-potential linear approximation for LQ differential games
Balint Varga, Gergely Lorant Kiss, Andreas Schwung
Feedback Nash equilibria of infinite-horizon linear-quadratic (LQ) differential games are characterized by coupled algebraic Riccati equations (cAREs), whose numerical solution generally relies on iterative algorithms and can be highly sensitive to their initialization. Motivated by the $α$-potential-game framework, this letter proposes an $α$-potential linear approximation for constructing a systematic, game-dependent initialization. For an N-player LQ game, a reference potential game is constructed. Its equilibrium requires solving only one standard algebraic Riccati equation. The original cAREs are subsequently linearized around this reference solution, yielding a coupled linear system whose solution provides player-specific corrections and hence an approximate feedback Nash equilibrium. The resulting approximation is used to initialize three standard cARE solvers. Numerical experiments on $10^4$ randomly generated two-player games show that the proposed initialization reduces the mean number of iterations. Further experiments for $N=2,\ldots,13$ show that the reduction in iteration count persists as the number of players increases.

We consider the convergence, worst-case complexity, and implementation of R2N, a modified quasi-Newton method for large-scale unconstrained smooth optimization. At each iteration, we compute a step that approximately minimizes the sum of a quadratic model of the objective with an adaptive quadratic regularization, and that results in sufficient decrease. The objective is only assumed to be $C^1$, although second derivatives may be used if they are available. The implementation features a broad range of step-computation strategies, from sparse factorization to matrix-free Krylov methods, that satisfy global convergence requirements. When detected, directions of nonpositive curvature are exploited. Our analysis allows unbounded model Hessians, provided they satisfy a mild growth condition. We derive a worst-case evaluation complexity bound that separates the progress made along positive- and nonpositive-curvature directions. By forcing the regularization parameter to vanish near isolated local minimizers, we obtain superlinear local convergence. The implementation specializes naturally to nonlinear least-squares problems. We provide a modular Julia implementation, and use it in a numerical study on the CUTEst test set that assesses the treatment of nonpositive curvature, the subproblem solver, the update of the regularization parameter, and direct versus iterative subproblem solves. An Armijo-Goldstein line search along nonpositive-curvature directions, MINRES-QLP as subproblem solver, and a regularization parameter driven to zero near a solution form our recommended configuration. With exact second derivatives, R2N is competitive with a trust-region method, solving slightly more problems with fewer objective and gradient evaluations. With convex models, the trust-region method performs as well or better.

☆ Compact Slack-Free Penalty Functions for Inequality Constraints in Higher-Order Unconstrained Binary Optimization

We construct exact slack-free penalty functions for upper- and lower-bound constraints on binary-encoded integers. Each function is constructed hierarchically from the threshold bits through a recursive addition-and-multiplication rule, and its correctness for arbitrary bit widths and representable thresholds is proved by mathematical induction. Equivalent explicit finite sum-product representations are also derived, enabling direct analysis of product-term count and polynomial degree. Interval constraints are obtained by adding the lower- and upper-bound penalties, while exclusion constraints are obtained by multiplying them. Compared with the trivial enumerative construction, the proposed method reduces the worst-case product-term count from linear to logarithmic in the representable range. Except at one non-vacuous boundary threshold for each bound, it also reduces both product-term count and degree. The resulting single-bound penalties have minimum positive value 1 and maximum value at most the bit width, which may simplify penalty-weight selection. The same construction also extends exactly to fixed-scale fractional variables through appropriate scaling of the integer thresholds.

The algorithm starts by generating an optimal integer base-stock policy, which at zero setup cost achieves the tight worst-case factor $\sqrt{2}$ relative to the optimal system cost. For positive setup costs, it uses the reorder point of this integer base-stock policy and an integer lot at the economic order quantity scale. The inclusion of ordinary base stock in the continuous-review capped base-stock family also improves that family's earlier asymptotic $1.79$ upper guarantee to a uniform $\sqrt{2}$ guarantee valid at every finite parameter vector. To establish these guarantees, we construct a computable lower bound on the zero-setup optimal cost by tracking units already on hand or committed for delivery. We then combine it with a bound on holding and setup costs required by batching to obtain the general-setup guarantee and instance-specific performance bounds for any admissible replenishment policy. In our numerical study, the largest estimated policy-cost-to-lower-bound ratios are about $1.59$ for our heuristic $(r, Q)$ policy and $1.47$ after joint optimization of $r$ and $Q$. The heuristic also performs well against the optimized policy: over the sampled instances, its median extra cost ranges from $2.33\%$ to $3.91\%$, depending on the setup cost.

Fixed shipment costs encourage large orders, while inventory and customer backlog costs favor frequent replenishment. We study the classical echelon stock $(R,nQ)$ policy: the downstream stage requests a fixed lot, the upstream stage orders an integer multiple of that lot, and transfers contain complete lots. The guarantee holds even when the selected policy pays a setup charge for every lot while the optimal benchmark pays only once per aggregate shipment. To obtain the guarantee, we use a common inventory calculation that allows independently chosen replenishment frequencies while respecting upstream material availability. We compare its optimized value, an upper bound on the best integer-ratio policy cost, with a novel lower bound on the optimal system cost that combines allocated single-stage costs with the minimum inventory cost when setup costs are zero. We also show that no uniform factor below $(1+\sqrt{3})/2\approx1.366$ is possible for the classical class. Existing numerical experiments place best-found classical policies within $22.7\%$ of an evaluated lower bound across three broad grids. The results quantify both the reliability and the limits of a simple operating rule and explain how shipment consolidation, replenishment timing, and flexibility affect its value.

♻ ☆ An accelerated multiobjective gradient flow with implicit Hessian-driven damping
Wen Jiang, Hao Luo
In this paper, we propose an accelerated multiobjective gradient flow with implicit Hessian-driven damping for unconstrained convex multiobjective optimization problems in a real Hilbert space. The continuous flow is formulated as a system of two first-order equations involving only a single multiobjective projection operator and suitable time-scaling factors. Formally, it can also be expressed as a second-order system with explicit multiobjective Hessian-driven damping, which corresponds to the usual Hessian-driven damping introduced by Alvarez et al. [J. Math. Pures Appl., 81(8):747--779, 2002]. The first-order formulation, however, involves no Hessian term and can be regarded as an extension of the Hessian-driven Nesterov accelerated gradient flow by Chen and Luo [arXiv:1912.09276, 2019]. Assuming that the objective gradients are Lipschitz continuous on bounded sets and that the common lower level sets are bounded, we establish global existence in finite dimensions under suitable time-scaling conditions. An a priori energy estimate confines the solutions to a fixed bounded set, and a Lyapunov argument yields fast decay of a merit function and the KKT residual. Under an additional bound on the time-scaling factors, the trajectory of every global solution converges weakly to a weak Pareto point. Numerical tests illustrate the rapid residual decay and reduced oscillations.
♻ ☆ When Does Reallocating a Sampling Budget Pay? Instance-wise Allocation for Neural Routing Solvers
Jinhyung Bae
Neural routing solvers sample many solutions per instance and keep the best, with the same number of samples for every instance. We measure how much a non-uniform split of the same total budget is worth and which property of a workload decides it. Best-of-k curves estimated by averaging random orderings of stored samples overstate the gain, and deciding on one half of the samples while evaluating on the other understates it; we use exact best-of-k curves, a U-statistic over all orderings. For three pretrained solvers (POMO, the Attention Model and Sym-NCO) on the traveling salesman problem, reallocation reduces the total optimality gap by at most 2.5% on the training distribution, so uniform allocation is close to optimal there. On workloads that mix in out-of-distribution instances it reduces the gap by 11.8-13.3% (1.1-1.8% of tour length) for the two solvers that degrade under the shift, and almost nothing for the one that does not. Across two heterogeneity mechanisms, three solvers, two confirmation collections and budgets of 25 to 200 samples per instance, the gain is predicted by the spread of difficulty within a workload, not its average. Allocating on a power-law curve fitted to twenty charged probe samples per instance recovers 88-93% of the uncharged optimum; successive halving does worse. A 2-opt local search, however, removes most of the gap at negligible cost, after which reallocation adds a few hundredths of a percent of tour length.

♻ ☆ From Consensus-Based Optimization to Evolution Strategies: Proof of Global Convergence

Consensus-based optimization (CBO) is a powerful and versatile zero-order multi-particle method designed to provably solve high-dimensional global optimization problems, including those that are genuinely nonconvex or nonsmooth. The method relies on a balance between stochastic exploration and contraction toward a consensus point, which is defined via the Laplace principle as a proxy for the global minimizer. In this paper, we introduce new CBO variants that address practical and theoretical limitations of the original formulation of this novel optimization methodology. First, we propose a model called $δ$-CBO}, which incorporates nonvanishing diffusion to prevent premature collapse to suboptimal states. We also develop a numerically stable implementation, the Consensus Freezing scheme, that remains robust even for arbitrarily large time steps by freezing the consensus point over time intervals. We connect these models through appropriate asymptotic limits. Furthermore, we derive from the Consensus Freezing scheme by suitable time rescaling and asymptotics a further algorithm, the Consensus Hopping scheme, which can be interpreted as a form of $(1,λ)$-Evolution Strategy. For all these schemes, we characterize for the first time the invariant measures and establish global convergence results, including exponential convergence rates.
♻ ☆ Towards sparse optimization over convex loops: Equivalence of Square Root Velocity distance and Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao

The Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) distance on $S^{2}$ has recently been shown to coincide with a classical elastic distance between $S^{2}$-immersions in the theory of Riemannian shape analysis. While this correspondence holds in dimension $2$, the analogous statement fails in general on $S^{1}$ and, in the case of convex curves, it cannot be derived from existing two-dimensional arguments. In this paper, we establish that for convex absolutely continuous immersions of $S^{1}$ in the plane, the shape distance induced by the square root velocity transformation (SRVT) is indeed equivalent to the WFR distance acting on their associated length measures. The proof exploits a monotonicity principle for optimal transport on the universal cover of the circle, which in turn guarantees the existence of an optimal reparametrization achieving the SRVT infimum and enables a one-dimensional unbalanced optimal transport reformulation. Motivated by this equivalence, we further investigate the role of sparsity in shape optimization problems formulated in terms of length measures and regularized by the WFR distance. We study quantitative stability of Brenier potentials and maps under changes of the target measure. Let $κ>0$, for a $κ$-strongly log-concave source $ρ$, possibly with a non-smooth potential, the normalized transport potentials satisfy \[ \left\Vert u_μ-u_ν\right\Vert _{L^{2}(ρ)}\leqslant\left( 1/κ\right) ^{1/2}W_{2}\left( μ,ν\right) \] for arbitrary targets with finite second moments. This readily yields a Poincaré inequality for $κ$-strongly log-concave sources. The coefficient $(1/κ)^{1/2}$ is shown to be optimal. The proof relies on a probabilistic interpretation of cell energies and the subsequent variance decomposition. Interpolation from potential to map then yields the map stability for targets in a common compact set, \[ \left\Vert T_μ-T_ν\right\Vert _{L^{2}(ρ)}\leqslant \operatorname{Const} \cdot W_{2}\left( μ,ν\right) ^{1/3}. \] Sharpness of the order for both the potential and map stability are established. This clarifies a long- standing limitation in topological embedding: representing distributions by their Brenier maps preserves convergence, but it need not preserve local distances.

In this paper, the concepts of Koopman observability, Koopman detectability, and Koopman--Luenberger observer of nonlinear systems are provided. By defining the Koopman semigroup on a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), the conditions for Koopman exponential detectability are established, which involves solving an operator Lyapunov inequality that only implicitly involves the infinitesimal generator of the Koopman semigroup. Through the use of a finite-horizon Yosida approximation of the Koopman generator and an empirical sampling operator, the data-driven solution of the observer gain can be reduced to a finite-dimensional subspace specified by the sample and hence fulfilled by convex semidefinite programming (SDP). The standard quadratic optimization problem consists of minimizing a quadratic form over the standard simplex. It has highly relevant applications ranging from portfolio optimization to machine learning. However, if the quadratic form is neither convex nor concave, this problem is NP-hard. We study a distributionally robust chance-constrained variant whose ambiguity set is a Wasserstein ball around the sampled distribution and make four contributions. First, although the problem is nonconvex in the decision variable, we exploit its linear dependence on the uncertain matrix to reduce the problem to a mixed-integer nonlinear optimization problem. Second, we show that a judicious choice of matrix norm---the entrywise maximum norm---makes this reformulation both exact and tractable, and we describe the induced worst-case distribution. Third, our formulation is, by construction, the minimization of the worst-case Value-at-Risk of the random quadratic form; this unifies it with existing frameworks for uncertain standard quadratic optimization problems, in particular under chance constraints, and we identify natural settings in which it collapses to a single deterministic instance. Finally, we report numerical experiments on positive definite and indefinite instances which quantify how the model parameters drive the optimal value and solution time, and expose the computational cost of indefiniteness.

The latter setup-cost condition extends beyond supplier setup-cost dominance: a retailer dispatch may incur a setup cost up to 50 percent higher than a supplier order's. Demand vectors are i.i.d. over periods with finite positive means, and demands of different retailers may be correlated. Each retailer selects the full cycle of its single-location plan or a shifted cycle of half its width, under an inflated setup cost, and the warehouse serves requests in arrival order, allowing partial shipments. The upper bound on the policy's cost includes each retailer's mirror cost, which prices the warehouse imbalance created by that retailer's batching. The upper and lower bounds share a pooled supplier problem and add one problem per retailer, giving a factor independent of all lead times and the number of retailers. For arbitrary nonnegative setup costs and associated retailer demands, a consolidation policy holds allocated stock until a dispatch threshold is met and gives a factor below 4.9. On 864 instances built from Walmart store sales, the simulated cost of an integer-rounded implementation of the FIFO policy averages 1.45 times the lower bound and reaches 1.75, and our analytical upper bound on its cost is below 1.94 times the lower bound; both ratios to the lower bound have nearly the same mean at every supplier lead time.

We apply the framework to the assemblage relaxation of two-player non-local games in general probabilistic theories. ♻ ☆ Coupled Stochastic Multigrid Reconstruction for Blind Ptychography
Borong Zhang, Junjing Deng, Yi Jiang, Zichao Wendy Di
Blind ptychography enables quantitative imaging when both the specimen and illumination probe are unknown, but modern data sets call for reconstruction methods that can assimilate many diffraction patterns while resolving structure across spatial scales. We introduce a coupled stochastic multigrid framework that addresses these requirements within a unified optimization construction. Rather than appending multigrid correction to an existing stochastic algorithm, the framework begins with a common surrogate for the local object and probe updates and connects these updates to minibatch consensus and coarse-grid correction through a unified residual analysis. This analysis establishes local control of the geometric-mean coupling and characterizes its extension across a grid hierarchy. The fine-grid construction yields the geometric-mean regularized Ptychographical Iterative Engine (GM-rPIE), while the inclusion of multilevel corrections yields the geometric-mean Multilevel-Adaptive-Guided Ptychographic Iterative Engine (GM-MAGPIE). Across nine synthetic configurations spanning scan overlap and Poisson noise, GM-MAGPIE achieves the lowest final object error at the prescribed budgets, while either GM-rPIE or GM-MAGPIE achieves the lowest probe error. Reconstructions of experimental test-pattern and integrated-circuit data further demonstrate the framework's applicability to measured X-ray data.

♻ ☆ Efficient Hessian-Free Methods for Multi-Objective Bilevel Optimization with a Nonconvex Lower-Level Objective
Yicong Jiang, Feihu Huang
Multi-objective bilevel optimization has wide applications in the AI area such as automated learning and multi-task meta-learning. Although some recent studies have investigated multi-objective bilevel optimization, many existing methods rely on the (strongly) convex lower level problems. In fact, these multi-objective bilevel learning problems are generally nonconvex, and particularly their lower level problems are nonconvex. To fill this gap, we propose a class of Multi-Objective Moreau Envelope based Hessian-free Algorithms (MOMEHA) for the multi-objective bilevel learning problems with a nonconvex lower level. Specifically, our method uses the Moreau envelope to formulate a multi-objective single-level relaxation that enforces lower-level first-order stationarity. In particular, our method retains computational advantages of being single-loop and Hessian-free in the multi-objective setting by incorporating a smooth weighted Tchebycheff scalarization. Furthermore, we propose a momentum variant of MOMEHA (i.e., MB-MOMEHA) for the stochastic multi-objective bilevel learning problems. Under the stated assumptions, we establish finite-iteration bounds on the Moreau gap and Pareto stationarity residuals under dynamically relaxed gap constraints in both deterministic and stochastic settings. Some experiments on few-shot meta-learning and neural architecture search demonstrate that our methods outperform the existing approaches in terms of Pareto front quality, validating their effectiveness and robustness.
comment: 55 pages
♻ ☆ Dynamic Programming for Indefinite Stochastic McKean-Vlasov LQ Control Problem under Input Constraints
Xun Li, Liangquan Zhang
In this note, we study a class of indefinite stochastic McKean-Vlasov linear-quadratic (LQ in short) control problem under the control taking nonnegative values. In contrast to the conventional issue, both the classical dynamic programming principle (DPP in short) and the usual Riccati equation approach fail. We tackle these difficulties by extending the state space from $\mathbb{R}$ to probability measure space, afterward derive the the corresponding the infinite dimensional Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman (HJB in short) equation. The optimal control and value function can be obtained basing on two functions constructed via two groups of novelty ordinary differential equations satisfying the HJB equation mentioned before. As an application, we revisit the mean-variance portfolio selection problems in continuous time under the constraint that short-selling of stocks is prohibited. The investment risk and the capital market line can be captured simultaneously.
♻ ☆ A Unified Theory of Solvability for Stochastic Linear-Quadratic Control Problems I: The Homogeneous Case
Hongwei Mei
The existing theory of stochastic linear-quadratic (LQ) optimal control problems focuses on open-loop and closed-loop solvability. For finite horizon problems, it is widely accepted that those two types of solvability are not equivalent in general, as demonstrated by explicit counterexamples. In contrast, they coincide in standard infinite-horizon formulations with constant coefficients under suitable stabilizability and integrability assumptions. This paper aims at challenging this well-established paradigm by developing a novel framework of closed-loop solvability, namely generalized closed-loop solvability, which removes the $L^2$-integrability constraint on the feedback strategies from the existing formulation. It will be proven that open-loop and generalized closed-loop solvability are equivalent and the classical closed-loop solvablity is a particular case only when the admissible feedback strategy is $L^2$-integrable over the time horizon. In other words, the previously established non-equivalence between open-loop and closed-loop solvability stems solely from the limitations of the classical formulation which requires the $L^2$-integrability of the admissible feedback strategies over the time-horizon. Therefore, this paper unifies the theory of the solvabilitiy for stochastic LQ control problems. Moreover, our results offer a novel insight to stochastic LQ control problems: open-loop/generalized closed-loop solvability is essentially equivalent to piecewisely local closed-loop solvability in the classical sense. The current paper is focused on homogeneous cases only and non-homogeneous cases will be studied in a subsequent paper.
♻ ☆ Convergence Rate of a Functional Learning Method for Conditional Stochastic Optimization
Noel Smith, Andrzej Ruszczynski
We consider a stochastic optimization problem involving two random variables: a context variable $X$ and a dependent variable $Y$. The objective is to minimize the expected value of a nonlinear loss functional applied to the conditional expectation $\mathbb{E}[f(X, Y,β) \mid X]$, where $f$ is a nonlinear function and $β$ represents the decision variables. We focus on the practically important setting in which direct sampling from the conditional distribution of $Y \mid X$ is infeasible, and only a stream of i.i.d. observation pairs $\{(X^k, Y^k)\}_{k=0,1,2,\ldots}$ is available. In our approach, the conditional expectation is approximated within a prespecified parametric function class. We analyze a simultaneous learning-and-optimization algorithm that jointly estimates the conditional expectation and optimizes the outer objective. Using a specially designed measure of non-optimality, combining the squared norm of the objective function's gradient and the mean square error of the auxiliary parametric model, we establish that the method achieves a convergence rate of order $\mathcal{O}\big(1/\sqrt{N}\big)$, where $N$ denotes the number of observed pairs. The rate holds in expectation when the auxiliary model is linear in its parameters, which includes linear architectures with bounded features, and in probability for general smooth models.
♻ ☆ Active Learning For Contextual Linear Optimization: A Margin-Based Approach
Mo Liu, Paul Grigas, Heyuan Liu, Zuo-Jun Max Shen
We develop the first active learning method for contextual linear optimization. Specifically, we introduce a label acquisition algorithm that sequentially decides whether to request the ``labels'' of feature samples arriving in an unlabeled data stream, where the labels correspond to the objective coefficients in the linear optimization problem. The label acquisition rule is guided by the decision loss induced by the predicted coefficients, known as the Smart Predict-then-Optimize (SPO) loss. Motivated by the structure of the SPO loss, our algorithm uses the distance to degeneracy as a margin-based criterion for label acquisition. The algorithm processes incoming feature samples in batches, acquiring within each batch only the labels of samples whose distance to degeneracy falls below a rejection threshold. We derive non-asymptotic bounds for direct SPO-loss minimization over a general hypothesis class and for surrogate-loss minimization over a linear prediction class. These bounds demonstrate that, under certain natural conditions, our margin-based active learning algorithm requires fewer labels than supervised learning to achieve the same excess population risk for the chosen training loss. We provide concrete examples in which these conditions hold under continuous (sub-)Gaussian noise. Finally, we present numerical evidence demonstrating the practical value of our approach in applications such as personalized pricing and shortest-path problems.
♻ ☆ The Polyhedral Structure of Energy Storage Operations: Convex Hull and Valid Inequalities
Juan M. Morales
Energy storage models rely on complementarity constraints to prevent simultaneous charging and discharging, which turn them into disjunctive, nonconvex programs. Their linear relaxations, widely used in power system operation and planning, often violate these constraints. This paper studies the polyhedral structure of the multi-period operational set of a storage unit with conversion losses. We characterize the extreme points of its convex hull and show that, over any sub-horizon, the maximum energy that can be charged, or discharged, during a subset of periods is a submodular function of that subset, computable by a greedy rule. This structure yields an exponential family of linear valid inequalities, which we strengthen with the continuous power variables, and for which we establish necessary and sufficient conditions to define facets of the convex hull. The family contains inequalities that strictly dominate the storage capacity inequalities available in the literature. We further develop a separation algorithm that computes all the coefficients of a cut in linear time and can be made exact over contiguous sets of periods, together with a lifting procedure for the cuts that fail a facet condition. In 2000 instances of energy arbitrage with negative prices, the linear relaxation strengthened with the separated cuts returns an optimal schedule, free of simultaneous charging and discharging, in every instance, mostly after a single round of separation, whereas the strongest linear relaxation in the literature charges and discharges simultaneously in 43% to 77% of them.
♻ ☆ Algorithms for Computing Set Tolerances: Theory, Computational Analysis and Applications
Gerold Jäger, Dmitrii Panasenko
The regular set tolerance is an important term in sensitivity analysis. For combinatorial sum problems, e.g., the Traveling Salesman Problem, Shortest Path Problem and Minimum Spanning Tree Problem, it determines how much the sum of the costs of the elements of a set can be increased while ensuring that all current optimal solutions remain optimal. The regular set lower tolerance determines how much the sum of the costs of the elements of a set can be decreased while ensuring that the objective value of the optimal solution is not changed. We investigate general methods for computing regular (upper and lower) set tolerances in combinatorial sum problems. For the upper tolerance, we present a linear programming approach, and for the lower tolerances, three linear programming approaches, where the last two are novel and lead to recursive procedures for computation of the lower tolerances of all subsets of the given ground set. We give new upper bounds for set lower tolerances. For both upper and lower tolerances, we give an exact formula for sets of cardinality 2 and 3. Furthermore, we computationally compare and analyze our introduced tolerance LPs. Finally, we consider the computation of tolerances for the Minimum Spanning Tree Problem, give a formula for single tolerances, a lower bound for regular set upper tolerances and an exact formula for regular set lower tolerances.

☆ Feedback-Linearised Trajectory Tracking via Model-Informed Robust Geometric DDPC
Pranav Gupta, Deepan Muthirayan, Ravi Banavar
Data-driven predictive control (DDPC) predicts system responses from recorded trajectories, but nonlinear dynamics can limit the accuracy of fixed linear predictors. This paper studies geometric robust DDPC for trajectory tracking of a fully actuated manipulator using model-based feedback linearisation. A mechanical model maps virtual acceleration commands into joint torques, while recorded data capture residual dynamics arising from imperfect model parameters. The controller minimises worst-case prediction error over an open Grassmannian ball centred at the fitted trajectory subspace. Simulations on a planar 2R manipulator under gravity compare the proposed method with double-integrator model predictive control (MPC) and direct regularised data-enabled predictive control (DeePC). Results show improved tracking over double-integrator MPC despite increased torque effort, while performance relative to DeePC depends on the reference trajectory.

☆ Multimodal Masked Diffusion Autoencoder for Modeling Impaired Driving CVPR 2027
John Gideon, Anshul Gupta, Megan Applegate-Kenton, Kayli Battel, Todd J Rowell, Patricio Reyes Gomez, Laporsha Dees, Emily Sumner, Avinash Balachandran, Guy Rosman
Human cognitive state (e.g., distraction, stress), gaze, and behavior interact with the driving environment in subtle ways that AI could use to assist drivers, but ground-truth labels for human cognitive state levels are costly to obtain at scale. We propose a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder, ID-MAE, that adds a self-supervised objective to impairment prediction: alongside predicting the impairment label as a masked token, it reconstructs masked gaze and trajectory. To probe the effects of different modalities and types of impairments on model inference, we introduce DIVERT, a driving-simulator dataset containing 103 hours of driving data (n = 109) with ten impairment inductions spanning cognitive, visual, and emotional states, recorded with gaze, vehicle state, and scene video. We demonstrate how ID-MAE affords significant improvements in impairment inference results on both the DIVERT dataset and existing datasets, and enables strong results in additional tasks, such as trajectory and gaze prediction. For location-matched pairs, our model achieves a paired AUC of 0.706 for impairment detection on DIVERT, compared to 0.590 without reconstruction loss, improving over existing baselines. We probe the design space in terms of input modalities, masking scheme, positional encoding, attention mechanism, and decoding. We also investigate the interaction between various impairments in training and inference, demonstrating that visually demanding distractions are separable from cognitive distractions. Code and data will be available upon acceptance.

☆ Learned versus Kinematic Trajectory Prediction under Reduced Observation Frequency
Nukhbala Gadzhiev, Alexander Morochko
Trajectory prediction models for automated driving are usually trained on data with a fixed sampling frequency, while positions received via vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication arrive at 1-10 Hz. We study whether a learned predictor that uses only the observation history keeps its advantage over constant velocity (CV) and constant acceleration (CA) models when the history frequency drops. On the Argoverse 2 motion forecasting dataset, the 5 s history of the focal agent was downsampled from 10 Hz to 5, 2, and 1 Hz, and the 6 s future was predicted without maps or neighboring agents. An LSTM-based recurrent neural network (RNN) trained for each frequency was compared with the same network trained at 10 Hz and applied to sparse histories after linear interpolation. Hypotheses and thresholds were fixed before training, the main RNNs were trained with ten seeds each, and results on 24,984 test scenarios have bootstrap confidence intervals over scenarios and seeds. The average displacement error of the frequency-specific RNN grew by 3.1% at 5 Hz, 10.1% at 2 Hz, and 20.3% at 1 Hz. Contrary to our hypothesis, its advantage over the better kinematic model did not vanish on straight motion and was 24-30% on both straight motion and turns at every frequency, while for pedestrians CV was more accurate. The 10 Hz model with interpolation was at most 1.3% less accurate than the frequency-specific model down to 2 Hz but 11.5% less accurate at 1 Hz. Each hypothesis was only partly supported.

☆ WoRD: Diffusion-Based Posterior Inference for Online Goal Recognition NeurIPS 2026
Almog Anschel, Sarah Keren
Goal recognition is the task of inferring an agent's intended goal from its observed behavior. Most existing work focuses on high-level symbolic recognition, abstracting away the continuous motion through which agents reach their goal. Methods that do reason over continuous trajectories rely on an explicit dynamics model that is hard to acquire and rarely transfers across settings. Neither approach explicitly learns how agents move toward each candidate goal, limiting accuracy on ambiguous trajectory prefixes where such knowledge is most needed. We present WoRD (Waypoint Recognition with Diffusion), which uses a learned trajectory prior to infer the agent's goal from partial observations. At each step, WoRD runs one warm-started denoising chain per candidate goal, steers each chain toward the observed trajectory through a closed-form log-likelihood gradient, and reweights the resulting samples by Bayes' rule into a calibrated posterior over goals. We evaluate WoRD on simulated robot settings, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories using four metrics targeting distinct failure modes. Across all three settings, the same inference procedure preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs through ambiguous prefixes where filter- and classifier-based observers collapse to a single mode or grow overconfident.

☆ Capability Composition in Heterogeneous Teams via Barrier-Guided Diffusion Sampling
Diana Laura Morales, Ruoyu Lin, Magnus Egerstedt, Fabio Pasqualetti
The agents in a heterogeneous team can cooperate to accomplish tasks that exceed their individual capabilities. The team trajectories for a cooperative task can be generated by a generative model, provided that the model has been trained on demonstrations of the agents cooperating. Yet, demonstrations of cooperation are costly and may not exist for tasks that the team has never performed. The conditions under which the agents can combine their capabilities, however, are physical properties of the team and are known before any demonstration is collected. We encode the conditions as constraints on the team trajectories, and we enforce the constraints while sampling from generative models trained on demonstrations of each agent alone. We prove that the proposed method can generate every team trajectory that satisfies the constraints, although the demonstrations contain no cooperation. Hence the constraints determine which team trajectories can be generated, and the demonstrations determine how likely each team trajectory is. Numerical results on two cooperative tasks show the effectiveness of the method, which generates cooperative team trajectories that satisfy the constraints and requires no retraining when agents join or leave the team. Finally, we implement the method on a multi-robot testbed.

Using the embodiment-agnostic tool-center-point (TCP) pose as the action space, we present TCP4D, a unified model in which a shared 4D scene representation both tracks observed TCP motion and generates future TCP trajectories. Given a monocular video and initial 2D TCP queries, the tracker directly recovers metric TCP poses in SE(3) and gripper states alongside scene geometry and camera parameters. The generator samples local features from the same 4D representation along the recovered TCP tracks, then combines them with robot observations and language instructions to predict future TCP states. Our new cross-embodiment augmentation pipeline converts existing RGB videos into demonstrations for alternative embodiments by retargeting the recovered motion and synthesizing the corresponding observations, without recorded source-robot states. Experiments show that the tracker achieves absolute trajectory errors of 7.60 and 16.07 mm on DROID and RoboLab and adapts to a new embodiment with only ten demonstrations. While gravity is often used in mobile robotics as a global constraint for Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) algorithms, most estimation methods rely on indirect observation of the gravity vector. In this paper, we propose the use of altimeter measurements to directly observe the direction of the gravity vector. We provide a theoretical evaluation of the estimation noise and validate it through extensive experimental data, along with an evaluation of the impact of intersensor distance on our gravity vector estimates. Experimental results demonstrate that a median error of $0.87^\circ$ on the tilt estimation can be achieved with our system in semi-static scenarios. Furthermore, we demonstrate the potential of this approach by comparing it with state-of-the-art methods based on Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs). We highlight that we achieve similar performance to that of IMU-based systems in highly dynamic scenarios and even outperform in specific cases of accelerometer measurement saturation. Finally, an additional experiment shows the potential use within a robotic system through the integration into an Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm.

A legged robot can learn to walk inside a learned simulator: a neural network that predicts the robot's next state and is run forward on its own predictions. They are usually trained and checked one step ahead, although a policy uses them for a hundred steps or more. We audit one published system end to end, without a GPU: the dynamics model of the Robotic World Model (RWM) for the ANYmal D quadruped, and the uncertainty estimate of its follow-up, RWM-U. We rebuilt the model to match the released code's outputs, losses and gradients exactly, measured 101 trained simulators, 200 compressed copies and 38 simulators of three other architectures, and trained policies inside simulators that we tested in a hand-built MuJoCo model of the robot. Training on the model's own rollouts beat one-step training at 368 steps on all ten held-out episodes (registered), although one-step training was better one step ahead. One-step checks therefore misjudge design choices: pruning 30% of the weights kept 90% of the model's skill one step ahead and 39% at 2 s. Ensemble disagreement ranked rollout error well (Spearman +0.90 at 100 steps), yet covered 4.6% of outcomes at one sigma, against 68% for a calibrated estimate, as each network's own variance collapses under the implemented loss. Two checks that need no recorded future ranked some pools of simulators well, but neither was shown better than 8-step error in a primary test. At the robot level, accuracy has not predicted walking: all 18 fine-tuned copies we tested predicted better than the released model one and eight steps ahead, yet 13 gave failing policies, and registered tests of whether any check ranks simulators by their policies were not settled. In a secondary test, running the authors' policy inside each simulator ranked them well. We also report nine of our own claims that we withdrew. Scope: one robot, one gait, simulated data, no hardware.

☆ CADENCE: Learning Acyclic Gaits for Model-Based Quadruped Locomotion
Owen Sullivan, Sourav Selvaraj, Mahdi Agheli
Model-based quadruped controllers usually step on a cyclic gait, which lifts the legs in a fixed order on a fixed period, wherever the safe footholds are. We present CADENCE, a learned step planner with a small action space. Every 40 ms, it picks one of at most 65 discrete choices: no step, or one leg's step to a safe foothold. It also predicts a swing time. We train CADENCE by reinforcement learning on top of a convex model predictive controller (MPC). Nothing prescribes a gait: there is no gait schedule, and the reward has no gait term, only a cost per step. The one structural constraint is that at most two legs may swing at once. The policy we analyzed developed an acyclic gait, with no fixed period or stepping order, yet it still paired diagonal legs. An inverse footstep model (IFM), fitted on a controller's logged steps, turns each foothold into a command. With only the IFM refitted, on fewer than 20,000 steps, CADENCE ran frozen on OCS2's nonlinear MPC. In simulated trials on a range of terrains (26% to 49% voids) and speeds (0.1 m/s and 0.2 m/s), it succeeded in 85.1% (mean of five seeds), against 67.8% for OCS2-Trot, 65.5% for OCS2-Single, and 39.6% in a static walk ablation of CADENCE. At 49% voids, it succeeded in 72.9%, against 43.0% for OCS2-Trot.

These results demonstrate that co-design is not a physical necessity for 6D magnetic levitation control. More broadly, control learning from simulated physics can find solutions beyond the reach of control engineering in demanding industrial domains. Source code and demonstration videos are publicly available at https://sites.google.com/view/magflow.

This paper examines this emerging area, agentic intelligence for the physical world, by treating the world as the program's test suite. We organize the discussion around three questions: how agents write programs for the physical world, how these programs are tested, and how agents learn from the results. We first trace how language models for robots and software engineering agents came together, ask which software testing practices carry over to physical tests, and describe each program by where it sits relative to the actuator and by what judges it. For writing, we cover programs that act as robot policies and programs that support policy learning by producing rewards, tasks, and training worlds. For testing, we examine what physical trials cost, what traces, learned judges, simulators, and formal checks can establish in their place, and what safety requires beyond task success. For learning, we discuss how tested programs are retained as experience, in skill libraries and in model weights. Finally, we turn to benchmarks and evaluation practice and outline open challenges. Writing programs is becoming cheap, while trustworthy evidence about what they do remains costly. Progress will therefore depend on a physical counterpart of continuous integration: verification cheap enough to run often, reliable enough to trust under search, and maintained alongside the experience it validates.

Collaboration promises to extend humanoid capabilities beyond what individual robots can achieve. However, realizing this potential requires coordinated whole-body interactions, coherent long-horizon planning, and precise synchronization across robots. We introduce Heave-Ho, a decentralized framework for long-horizon collaborative multi-humanoid loco-manipulation. At the low level, we develop a multi-agent post-training framework that adapts a humanoid foundation tracking model to physically coupled interactions between humanoids, enabling coordinated decentralized control from local observations alone. At the high level, we train a vision-language planner and design a speech-based leader-follower coordination mechanism to synchronize decentralized execution without network communication. Trained with two identical humanoids, our system scales to teams of up to ten robots and generalizes to heterogeneous teams without retraining. To benchmark these capabilities, we introduce HH-Bench, comprising 12 tasks involving teams of 2 to 10 humanoids, including heterogeneous teams. Systematic evaluations show that Heave-Ho consistently outperforms baseline methods, while real-world experiments demonstrate robust decentralized collaboration across challenging tasks.

☆ ALERT: Extending Humanoid Motion Trackers with a General and Lightweight Human Avoidance Pipeline
Zhaoyang Li, Chiyu Zhang, Chengxin Xu, Peng Yang, Zhonghao Guo, Wanting Li, Ziyu Chen
Whole-body motion tracking has enabled humanoid dancing, athletic motions, and teleoperation, providing a foundation for capability demonstrations and manipulation data collection. However, existing tracking policies lack awareness of nearby humans and proactive avoidance capabilities, while motion substitution and local constraint-based corrections may compromise reference motion integrity and tracking continuity. We propose ALERT, a general lightweight pipeline for extending motion tracking to shared human-robot environments. Through lightweight adaptation, it integrates human perception and proactive avoidance into pretrained tracking policies, balancing avoidance demands with reference motion tracking while preserving existing motion capabilities. Simulation and real-world experiments across tracking backbones demonstrate reliable collision-free execution through localized human avoidance, preserving whole-body coordination and enabling rapid recovery of reference tracking, while retaining the ability of pretrained policies to track unseen motions.
☆ From Temperature-Limited to Battery-Limited Legged Locomotion
Raphaël Ségas, Balázs Opra, Léo Ghafari, Thomas Stewart
On legged robots, sustained locomotion often ends in thermal shutdown rather than battery depletion: the heat of walking concentrates in a few joint motors, which overheat long before the battery is empty. We train thermally aware locomotion policies by reinforcement learning without ever observing temperature, and demonstrate this on a Unitree Go2 quadruped. We first identify a coupled 13-node lumped RC thermal network, fitted on two runs of a single robot and calibrated against the measured electrical power, that predicts all twelve motor temperatures with a mean RMSE below 1 $^\circ$C across different robot instances, gaits, payloads, and speeds. Under a sustained gait, the temperatures the motors will settle at follow directly from the gait-averaged squared torques and joint speeds. Our core contribution is a reward that drives down the hottest predicted asymptotes: thermal time constants exceed the credit-assignment horizon of reinforcement learning by orders of magnitude, but predicted asymptotes respond to torque and joint speed within a single gait cycle, so the policy learns to lower and spread heat with no temperature input. On the robot, the policy turns sustained locomotion from temperature-limited to battery-limited: with a 5 kg payload at 1 m/s, a learned baseline reaches thermal shutdown after 19 minutes (1.1 km), whereas our policy runs the battery down after 174 minutes (10.0 km) with its hottest motor 14 $^\circ$C below the shutdown threshold in a 26 $^\circ$C room; on an unloaded factory circuit with stairs and ramps, the baseline overheats after 25 laps (6.2 km), while our policy completes 47 (11.2 km) on one battery with 22 $^\circ$C of margin.

Underwater visual systems often suffer from blurry textures and low color contrast due to the inevitable light propagation. These issues can significantly degrade the perception of stable robotic operations. In this paper, we introduce a novel learning-based sensing system that tackles the multidimensional vision tasks in underwater; concretely, we deal with image enhancement, depth estimation, and uncertainty for 3-D visual systems. Also, we propose a TRIDENT model in a fast and lightweight manner; TRIDENT consists of three parallelized decoders and one backbone structure for efficient feature sharing. In addition, it is designed to be trained to express complex parameterization. In experimental evaluation on several standard datasets, we demonstrate that TRIDENT significantly outperforms other existing methods on image enhancement and depth estimation. Despite performing three tasks, our model has better efficiency than the others for both memory size and inference time. Finally, our joint learning approach demonstrates robustness in feature matching and seamlessly extends from 2-D to 3-D vision tasks. Supplements are available at https://sites.google.com/view/underwater-trident/home

☆ Haptic Probing for Subsurface-Aware Force Distribution on Layered Soft Tissue
Lei Shi, Xiaoyu Wang, Cheng Zhou, Yongjian Liu, Jing Wang, Dongsheng Zhang, Yonghui Zhu, Xiong Li
Force-regulated contact with layered soft tissue fails most often where the subsurface composition changes: controllers infer the substrate from the loading signal alone, so the estimate guiding them lags the change---more acutely, we argue, over compliant than over bone-backed tissue. We remove that lag with a separate haptic channel. Under a light preload, a brief low-amplitude excitation lets the local dynamic admittance discriminate muscle from bone-backed tissue relative to a per-subject baseline, before task force is applied---active haptic sensing used to commit a control decision rather than to characterise tissue. A force- and tactile-driven distribution law then consumes that regime throughout execution: an instantaneous allocation equalises pressure across the engaged fingertips, while the regime sets the admissible pressure and hence the area the hand must recruit to deliver the target force---making patch area a controlled variable rather than a by-product. Probing, switches and recruitment are priced in a partitioned passivity budget, so safety monitoring cannot suppress the probe and a refused recruitment forfeits force tracking rather than the pressure bound. We report force tracking and pressure uniformity over curved, migrating contact on three human subjects, with regime labels from anatomical landmarks.
☆ CueClash: Frontier Vision-Language Models Judge 3-D Relations Close to the Picture Plane
Soham Dan
A vision-language model (VLM) can judge 3-D relations from the picture or from the ground layout. In photographs the two usually agree. We separate them with CueClash, rendered scenes in which the 2-D cue for each of five relations is right on exactly half the statements. The shortcut gap is accuracy when the cue is right minus accuracy when it is wrong. For Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.6 Flash at low reasoning effort it is +18 to +37 percentage points. It is +7 to +29 without two relations whose cue-wrong items are confounded with borderline cases or occlusion. Given ground coordinates and each relation's definition, they answer 99 to 100% correctly. Pixel measurements with camera depths remove most of the gap for objects fitting through openings. The failure lies in the step from the picture to the layout. The maps that the models draw of the scene from above mostly keep the depth order but, like the picture, shorten depth. GPT-5.5's maps stay close to a copy of the picture. Opus 5.5's and Gemini's maps undo about 0.6 of this shortening. Gemini's then shrink all depths by a further uniform factor. Opus 5.5 follows the picture mainly on fits, and its maps correct depth about as much as human observers of real scenes do. The three models also lose accuracy on CV-Bench photographs where a reliable 2-D cue misleads. In two open models the layout information reaches the language model, but their maps lose much of it.

Multimodal agents can now control robot arms by calling tools and writing code. Existing benchmarks fall short in three ways: most test one or two arms on short tasks, many pause the world while the agent thinks, and many give it ground-truth object positions. We present RoboTeam, a simulated benchmark where agents control 4 to 16 robot arms in real time from camera images alone. Its 36 tasks are long jobs that the arms must do together, such as passing timbers or building a picture from hundreds of cubes. We start from the most flexible agent system, the adaptive system, where one agent decides when to fork delegates. With it, gpt-6.1-sol and opus-5.5 complete 28 and 27 tasks, and four other models at most 3. But at a high price: a typical task takes gpt-6.1-sol 3.5 hours and 218 million input tokens, and a third of its steps fail at least once and must be retried. We then compare it with three fixed systems: single-agent, hierarchical, and decentralized. All four complete a similar number of tasks but differ in time and tokens. The hierarchical and decentralized systems are faster but use up to 1.9 times the tokens, and the single agent uses fewer tokens but takes 1.6 times as long, so the adaptive system lies between them. Even so, no model or system is yet fast, cheap, and reliable at once. RoboTeam measures these limits where earlier benchmarks cannot: long multi-arm jobs, camera images only, and a world that never pauses.

☆ DailyBrick: Language-Guided Synthesis of Brick Assembly Instructions
Hang Zhang, Qijian Tian, Yuan Xie, Xuhong Wang, Xin Tan
Generating a LEGO model from a user request is more than a plausible 3D shape generation. LEGO models require physical support per brick, and each brick should be placed unblocked. Current methods address this issue by training an expert large language model. We reduce the problem of generating extremely long context on all brick connections to that of writing a program that builds LEGO models like a human, considering each intermediate step could be executed. We introduce DailyBrick , a multi-stage agentic system that produces a LEGO model together with a brick-by-brick assembly instruction for human building and robot assembly. We design a multi-stage harness with roles to help LLMs generate more effectively. A versioned construction SDK compiles multi-level decisions, from semantic subparts to individual bricks, into canonical operations. An external Meta-Reviewer agent replays and inspects the generated package, verifies the model and its construction process, identifies failures, traces them to the responsible stage, and routes them to bounded repairs or to editable candidates for later skill or tool updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DailyBrick generates LEGO models based on simple user requests better than recent agentic systems, and show its utility in downstream applications such as robot manipulations on model assembly from instructions and brick sets (https://SpatialAgent.github.io/DailyBrick/).
☆ Low-speed Limit Cycle Walking of Planar X-shaped Bipedal Robot with Special Properties
Fumihiko Asano, Cong Yan
This paper proposes a novel planar semicircular-footed X-shaped bipedal robot in which the center of mass of each leg link is at the same position as the hip joint, and discusses a method for generating a stable limit cycle gait on level ground. First, we outline the assumptions of the robot model with four degrees of freedom, and develop the mathematical equations of motion and collision. Second, we set the relative hip-joint angle as a control output and design a control system to follow it to the desired trajectory specified as a fifth-order function of time. Third, we mathematically show that there are special properties: the angular velocity of the swing leg does not change before and after the collision, and the time-integral of the control input becomes zero in a steady gait. We also mathematically show that the model has the feature that approximate linearization is effective and the antigravity effect of semicircular feet can be utilized. Through numerical simulations, we verify the validity of the theoretical results, and analyze some fundamental gait properties such as convergence speed and mechanical energy restoration.

☆ CRA: Continuous Risk Assessment for Safety-critical Visual Navigation
Lihao Zheng, Ying Wu, Chen Jiang, Randy Freeman
Traditional safety-critical control methods often rely on predefined constraints that separate states into safe and unsafe regions. While recent studies have extended geometric safety toward semantic safety, real-world safety is rarely purely binary. The risk associated with an object or human can vary continuously with its physical properties, like motion, and interaction context; for example, a person carrying a heavy object or a hot object moving at high speed may require a different safety response from an ordinary static obstacle. In this paper, we propose a vision-based continuous risk assessment framework for safety-critical visual navigation. Our method uses RGB and LiDAR observations to estimate four risk factors (kinetic, potential, contact-severity, and thermal) and combines them into a continuous risk score for each assessed object or person. These estimates are integrated into a Poisson safety function with a Laplace guidance field as a safety filter, enabling online monitoring and intervention in open-world robot navigation. We demonstrate the proposed method in a simulated restaurant scene.

☆ ReLAP: Latent Action Pretraining through Recurrent Video Prediction in JEPA Space
R. Gnana Praveen, Ali Rouzbayani, Zhiying Jiang, Bidhan Roy
Videos provide a rich source of physical interaction for learning robot behavior without action annotations, yet effective latent actions must capture not only local transitions but also how those transitions evolve over time. A shared inverse dynamics model infers compact continuous latent actions from adjacent observations, while a latent world model recurrently predicts the future JEPA features. Because each predicted feature becomes the context for the next transition, errors at later steps backpropagate through the rollout to earlier latent actions, encouraging temporally coherent dynamics beyond pairwise reconstruction. We transfer this representation to a vision-language model using two complementary objectives: latent distillation from the frozen inverse teacher and recurrent future-feature prediction through the frozen latent world model. The resulting policy is then adapted to robot demonstrations with action flow matching. At deployment, the explicit latent-action and world-model branches are removed, and the fine-tuned VLM predicts physical actions directly, reducing inference complexity. With only 11M pretraining samples and 1.06B trainable parameters, ReLAP achieves 97.9% on standard LIBERO and 70.0% over zero-shot LIBERO-Plus perturbations. On the LARY latent-action benchmark, ReLAP ranks second in both mean regression error and mean classification accuracy among the compared methods. These results demonstrate that recurrent action-free latent action pretraining can learn compact, temporally structured, and transferable representations for downstream robot control.

Noise steering improves pretrained generative robot policies by learning to select their initial noise without updating model weights. We find that actions in the evaluated world-action models are more sensitive to video noise than action noise, making video noise an expressive input for steering. However, the noise-steering methods we evaluate, in their published forms, struggle to scale to the high-dimensional noise inputs of large policy classes such as world-action models. This separates the actor's control dimension from the full noise dimension, enabling steering of both video and action inputs. Across three world-action models and ten model-task pairs, video steering improves average success by 26.2 percentage points over the base policy, compared with 7.1 points for DSRL action steering. For smaller action policies, the same construction achieves comparable final success while generally improving early-training success. Steering actors trained in simulation also transfer to three physical bimanual manipulation tasks across two base policies, without additional real-world training.

A frozen latent world model combined with sampling-based model predictive control is a visual planner. At deployment, the executed action can depart from the commanded one, and the frozen model has no way to notice. We show that the model can be run in reverse: for any hypothesized actuation shift, it predicts what it should have observed under that shift, and comparing this prediction with what was actually observed quantifies the shift and lets the planner correct itself. Unlike the residual energy, which mixes the shift with the model's own error, the score keeps only the part of the residual that a shift can produce. This shift score detects the shift with a locally optimal test, estimates it with Cramer-Rao error bars, names the dominant generator, and compensates the planner once an alarm fires. On PushT, TwoRoom and OGBench-Cube with a frozen latent world model, measured detection follows the prediction to within 0.05 AUROC. On a real robotic arm, the score identifies a base-joint offset that no joint encoder registers and reduces the reach error from 36 mm to 3-5 mm, and under shifts drawn at random and sealed before the session, estimates recover 92-94% of the error reduction achieved with the true shift. The broader implication is that a frozen world model can act as a filter by predicting the future, testing action-interface uncertainty and validity, and finally correcting failures.

As a result, many of the behaviors we most want robots to run, from learned policies to aggressive maneuvers at the limits of traction, cannot be certified at all. To decide when to switch, we derive the contraction insertion gradient, the first-order effect of a recovery insertion on the certificate, and embed it in a switching-time program in which feasibility alone guarantees safety and optimality only shapes performance. To supply the certificates, we develop sequential convex synthesis that monotonically grows the certified tube toward the exact viability kernel. We validate our approach in simulated quadrotor flight through uncertain obstacles, where it outperforms invariance-based safety filters, and in hardware deployments aboard a full-scale IndyNXT autonomous racecar, where it repeatedly recovers the car from an aggressive raceline at the limits of handling in the rain. Recoverability provides a certified exit strategy, extending formal safety guarantees to aggressive, learned, and experimental behaviors without requiring their invariance.

SPICE also achieved branch manipulation beyond the reactive controller and remained effective under visual occlusion, where the image-conditioned DP failed. For six frozen DINO and V-JEPA encoders, feature distance barely tracks the object's distance to its goal: the rank correlation is at most 0.11, against 0.87 for object-mask centroids. It is dominated by background and robot patches, and frozen-feature readouts capture the arm far better than the object. Used as a planning cost, the learned representation places the object in 15 of 21 tasks, as many as an oracle that reads the true object position, while mask geometry reaches 10 and frozen feature distance 9. It still solves the most tasks when the unseen robot arm is visible, and its ranking transfers to held-out layouts with unseen object instances and categories without any adaptation.

The grammar provides a compact representation, and its arbitration decisions can be recovered from geometric containment (agreement 0.905 +/- 0.062 across 10 seeds, versus 0.611 +/- 0.090 for a Euclidean control). These results show how typed grammars can make robot generation more interpretable and geometrically coordinated, without implying that every feasible design will locomote or that grammar-based search universally outperforms generic optimizers.

The model combines a floating-base coupled oscillator network (FBCON), whose latent potential energy depends only on the DLO's shape, with a learned affine diffeomorphism $Φ$ between observed positions along the DLO and latent coordinates. Its shape dynamics are stable by construction, and its Lagrangian structure yields explicit expressions for kinetic and potential energy. We exploit this structure to design a model-based proportional-derivative (PD) controller that compensates for the learned potential forces, thereby establishing closed-loop stability guarantees and ensuring convergence. We evaluate the approach on four simulated DLOs and a real bimanual robot setup. In simulation, $Φ$-CON achieves prediction accuracy comparable to neural ordinary differential equation (NODE) models and Lagrangian neural networks (LNNs), with $97.2\%$ and $90.2\%$ fewer parameters, respectively. Relative to a model-free PD baseline, the proposed controller reduces mean endpoint regulation error by $97.5$-$99.7\%$ in simulation and achieves a mean per-target reduction of $27.9\%$ across both endpoints in real-world experiments, demonstrating the importance of explicitly accounting for the mechanical response of stiff and heavy objects.

Finally, qualitative tests highlight the robot's locomotion in cluttered, real-world environments. The model and experiments presented in this work can inform future designs of space-constrained jump mechanisms in centimeter-scale robots for search and rescue and inspection in unstructured environments.

☆ RageVLA: Augmentation-Trained Perception and Action for State-of-the-Art Robustness on LIBERO

Vision-language-action (VLA) models look saturated on LIBERO, yet most of them fall apart on LIBERO-PRO as soon as an object moves or the instruction asks for something new. In the data, LIBERO demonstrations are re-arranged by general rules: every object and fixture is moved and rotated, tasks are carried into other environments and onto other surfaces, and every instruction is paraphrased. In the policy, a perception engine on frozen DINOv3 features, trained on this augmented data, hands the action model the scene in decoupled form: a list of objects with their positions, and a compact code of what the gripper is looking at, next to image and instruction embeddings from TinyCLIP. A flow-matching diffusion transformer, trained from scratch, acts on this view. We call this combination of Robust Augmentation and Grounded Encoding RageVLA. With 0.21 billion parameters, RageVLA sets a new state of the art on LIBERO-PRO among VLA policies, scoring 0.72 against 0.53 for the best published model, and a larger variant reaches 0.73. Two further tests on LIBERO-Object show that the policy acts on what it perceives. When the object positions it is given are shuffled while the camera images stay correct, its success falls from 0.965 to 0.215. When the target object is displaced by 28 cm, it still succeeds in 0.865 of the episodes, where $π_{0.5}$, run through the same harness, succeeds in 0.105.

☆ Learning and Control in Physically Coupled Dynamical Systems

We introduce TAG (Testbed for Autonomous Games), a compact, low-cost robotic platform for studying learning and control in physically coupled dynamical systems. TAG combines an actively tilted and steered ball-in-maze board with a top-mounted rotary inverted pendulum. The pendulum's reaction torque and vibration disturb the board and marble, while the board's tilt, driven by the maze-solving policy, simultaneously disturbs the pendulum's balance. The main challenge in learning control policies for each subsystem is accounting for the impact of one subsystem's dynamics on the other's learning process. To address this challenge, we present complementary reinforcement learning paradigms, leveraging model-based and model-free approaches to learn the control policies for the maze and pendulum, respectively. Our key finding is that introducing the pendulum causes an immediate, sharp drop in the maze policy's success rate, but the policy adapts online and recovers to its pre-coupling performance within a small number of learning episodes. Experimental results show that both policies, trained independently, successfully control the maze board and the pendulum despite their physical coupling.
☆ BiCAT: Bimanual Coordination Action Tokenization

Autoregressive vision-language-action (VLA) models predict discrete action tokens with the next-token objective of their vision-language backbone, so the action tokenizer defines the interface between the policy and the robot. In bimanual manipulation, the two arms share a repertoire of movements yet coordinate through complementary roles, and an action representation should capture both. However, most existing tokenizers encode both arms as a single concatenated action vector, in which motion patterns common to the two arms are not shared and cross-arm dependencies remain entangled within each token. The policy must therefore learn both aspects implicitly. We propose Bimanual Coordination Action Tokenization (BiCAT), which shares one motion representation across arms while conditioning each arm's tokens on its partner through symmetric cross-arm attention and a joint decoder. The policy then predicts all tokens of each arm in parallel, generating the left arm first and the right arm conditioned on it. Across ten RoboTwin 2.0 tasks and six real-world tasks on three embodiments, BiCAT achieves the highest success among the compared tokenizers. In simulation, it improves mean success by 17.6 percentage points over the strongest of eight baselines, with the largest gains on tasks that require close coordination between the arms, while requiring only 40.5 ms per action chunk. These results suggest that the action tokenizer is a natural place to model bimanual coordination.
☆ Hebbian self-organization of monosynaptic reflexes in a biologically realistic multiarticular limb
Jonathan Realmuto, Erfan Nozari, Gerald E. Loeb
Spinal monosynaptic reflexes depend on patterns of connectivity between muscle spindle afferents and motoneurons that should reflect musculoskeletal dynamics. One possibility is that the details of these circuits are specified genetically, but this requires an unlikely coevolution of musculoskeletal and neural elements. Here we show how biomechanical structure can determine the connectivity of self-organized spinal circuits. Using a neuromechanical model combining a multi-joint limb, proprioceptive feedback, and Hebbian plasticity driven by motor babbling, we find that biologically realistic connectivity emerges spontaneously when babbling is neither too sparse nor too frequent. This results in strong homonymous projections, weaker heteronymous projections among functional synergists, and very weak connections among antagonists. This outcome also depends on musculoskeletal morphometry. Heteronymous synergies form when proximal muscles are strongest---the characteristic gradient of mammalian limbs--whereas excessively strong biarticular muscles lead to unphysiological antagonist coupling. The mechanisms differ: homonymous connections arise from direct sensorimotor correlation during fusimotor coactivation by beta motoneurons, while heteronymous connections depend on multi-joint dynamics that emerge only after homonymous reflexes stabilize and increasing muscle strength generates multisegmental motion. Overall, this study provides a mechanistic basis for fetal sensorimotor development and generates testable predictions about the consequences of naturally occurring and experimentally induced variations.

Nikhil X. Bhattasali, Jaron Cui, Lerrel Pinto, Grace W. Lindsay
Animals generate behavior through continuous interactions between their neural circuits, bodies, and environment. Embodied simulations study these interactions by testing neural circuit models in biologically realistic settings. Recent efforts have simulated diverse animals, and emerging work on biologically grounded neural architectures has begun to integrate circuit connectivity and single-unit dynamics from experimental data into artificial neural networks, introducing stronger inductive biases and closer mechanistic alignment with biology. How can we develop embodied simulations that enable the study of increasingly complex bodies and neural circuits? In this work, we address the challenge through coordinated advances in the simulated body, neural architecture, and training infrastructure. We introduce Rat v2, an efficient and flexible biomechanical body for simulating rat behavior. To control this body, we develop Rat NCAP, a biologically grounded neural architecture for locomotion based on mammalian spinal circuits that incorporates cell-type-specific connectivity and a novel flexor-extensor neuromechanical interface. To optimize circuit parameters, we develop GPU-accelerated simulation and training infrastructure. The model learns to locomote at different speeds and transition between gaits without imitation learning, producing locomotion statistics, kinematics, and cell-type-specific neural activity consistent with experimental data. Analyses reveal that the neuromechanical interface substantially affects trainability and gait quality, and in silico cell-type ablations reproduce known gait phenotypes and predict gait changes under graded perturbations. Together, these findings support the view that embodied simulations at an intermediate level of abstraction can simultaneously reproduce complex behavior and yield mechanistic insights into the neural circuits that generate it.
