A first difference compared to other existing introductions to SDP is that this work comes out of a mind that was itself struggling to understand. This may seem to be only a weakness, but, paradoxically, it is both a weakness and a strength. First, I did not try to overpower the reader, but I tried to minimize the distance between the author and the reader as much as possible, even hoping to achieve a small level of mutual empathy. This enabled me avoid a quite common pitfall: many long-acknowledged experts tend to forget the difficulties of beginners. Other experts try to make all proofs as short as possible and to dismiss as unimportant certain key results they have seen thousands of time in their career. I also avoided this, even if I did shorten a few proofs when I revised this manuscript two years after it was first written. However, I also kept certain proofs that seem longer than necessary because I feel they offer more insight; an important goal is to capture the "spirit" of each proven result instead of reducing it to a flow of formulae. The very first key step towards mastering SDP programming is to get full insight into the eigen-decomposition of real symmetric matrices. It is enough to see the way many other introductions to SDP programming address this eigen-decomposition to understand that their target audience is different from mine. They often list the eigen-decomposition without proof, while I give two proofs to really familiarize the reader with it.
comment: 100 pages
♻ ☆ Entropic smoothing and gradient approximation for Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization
Tam Le
Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization offers a framework for model fitting in machine learning under potential shifts in the data distribution. We study a regularized variant of this problem in which entropic smoothing produces a sampled approximation of the original objective. We establish convergence of the approximate gradients to subgradients of the unregularized objective as the regularization parameter vanishes, enabling convergence guarantees for stochastic gradient methods. We obtain qualitative convergence results under general assumptions and provide convergence rates under additional regularity. In particular, we prove rates for the convergence of the unregularized objective values, up to sampling errors, when the regularization level is decreased across iterations. Our analysis also yields results of independent interest on approximating the subdifferentials of maximum functions by gradients of their smooth approximations, together with growth-based lower bounds on optimal dual variables in Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization.
♻ ☆ A Spectral Proximal DC Algorithm with Nonmonotone Line Search and Extrapolation
Kelin Wu, Hongpeng Sun
The paper proposes a novel proximal difference-of-convex (DC) algorithmic framework to solve general nonconvex, nonsmooth optimization problems. The basic pBBDCA method combines Barzilai-Borwein (BB) parameter selection with a nonmonotone directional line search, requiring only one proximal solve per iteration. We also develop two extrapolated variants using restart and safeguarding mechanisms. The global convergence of the proposed framework is rigorously established under the Kurdyka-Łojasiewicz property. Numerical experiments on the SCAD-regularized least squares problem and graph Ginzburg-Landau image segmentation models demonstrate that the proposed methods achieve highly competitive efficiency and accuracy.
♻ ☆ Transferability of Error Bounds and the Kurdyka-Łojasiewicz Property under $C^1$ Partial Smoothness
Hanju Wu, Ching-pei Lee, Yue Xie
This work studies how a generalized error bound (GEB) property in the ambient Euclidean space transfers to the active manifold under $C^1$ partial smoothness. The GEB generalizes the standard error bound, which upper bounds the distance to a subset of critical points using first-order stationarity residuals, by allowing the distance to be composed with a gauge function. In the ambient space, these residuals are measured by the subdifferential or the slope of the original function, while on the manifold they are measured by the Riemannian gradient or the slope of the restricted function. We develop complementary geometric and metric analyses to show that the ambient and manifold GEBs are equivalent with the same gauge function. The geometric argument shows that the projection of the subdifferential onto the tangent space coincides with the Riemannian gradient, while the metric approach combines slope estimates, identifiability, and a new uniform linear-growth result for $C^1$ manifolds. We further extend our analysis to establish the analogous equivalence for the Kurdyka--Łojasiewicz (KL) property, with the same desingularizer, and separately characterize their connections with the GEB. Finally, for regularized optimization, we relate subdifferential and proximal error bounds, thereby placing the previously established equivalence between proximal and manifold error bounds for $\ell_1$-regularization within a broader framework.
♻ ☆ Markov Decision Processes of the Third Kind: Learning Distributions by Policy Gradient Descent
Nicole Bäuerle, Athanasios Vasileiadis
The goal of this paper is to analyze distributional Markov Decision Processes as a class of control problems in which the objective is to learn policies that steer the distribution of a cumulative reward toward a prescribed target law, rather than optimizing an expected value or a risk functional. To solve the resulting distributional control problem, we propose a policy-gradient algorithm based on neural-network parameterizations of randomized Markov policies, defined on an augmented state space and a sample-based evaluation of the characteristic-function loss. Under mild regularity and growth assumptions, we prove convergence of the algorithm to stationary points using stochastic approximation techniques. Several numerical experiments illustrate the ability of the method to match complex target distributions, recover classical optimal policies when they exist, and reveal intrinsic non-uniqueness phenomena specific to distributional control.
♻ ☆ A generalized Hurwitz stability criterion via rectangular block Hankel matrices for nonmonic matrix polynomials
Zixiang Ni, Yongjian Hu, Xuzhou Zhan
We develop a Hurwitz stability criterion for nonmonic matrix polynomials via column reduction, generalizing existing approaches constrained by the monic assumption and thus serving as a more natural extension of Gantmacher's classical stability criterion via Markov parameters. Starting from redefining the associated Markov parameters through an adaptive column-wise Lienard-Chipart splitting method, our framework constructs two structured matrices whose rectangular Hankel blocks are obtained via the extraction of these parameters. We establish an explicit interrelation between the inertia of column reduced matrix polynomials and the derived structured matrices. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Hurwitz stability of column reduced matrix polynomials can be determined by the Hermitian positive definiteness of these rectangular block Hankel matrices.
♻ ☆ Optimal Oracle Complexity for Weakly Convex Optimization
Jiajin Li, Siyu Pan
We study the oracle complexity of finding $ε$-stationary points of $ρ$-weakly convex and $G$-Lipschitz functions, where stationarity is measured by the gradient norm of the Moreau envelope. We consider an exact first-order oracle that returns both the function value and the full subdifferential at every query point. For sufficiently small $ε>0$, we prove that every first-order algorithm, including randomized algorithms, requires $Ω({ρG^2Δ}/{ε^4})$ oracle queries to succeed with any fixed positive probability, where $f(0)-\inf f\leΔ$. This lower bound matches the best known deterministic and stochastic first-order upper bounds, up to universal constants, and establishes the optimal randomized and deterministic first-order oracle complexity. The result separates smooth nonconvex and nonsmooth weakly convex optimization: the additional $ε^{-2}$ factor is intrinsic to nonsmooth geometry rather than to stochastic oracle noise.
comment: 28 pages, 1 figure. This version extends the lower bound to randomized first-order algorithms and a substantially broader initial-gap regime, with revised proofs and exposition
♻ ☆ A generalized alternating NGMRES method for PDE-constrained optimization problems governed by transport equations
Yunhui He, Andreas Mang
We propose a generalized alternating nonlinear generalized minimal residual method (GA-NGMRES) to accelerate first-order optimization schemes for PDE-constrained optimization problems governed by transport equations. Interpreting the update rule of a gradient descent scheme in the Hilbert space induced by the regularization model, i.e., a Sobolev gradient descent, as a fixed-point (FP) iteration, GA-NGMRES periodically alternates NGMRES updates with FP steps. It requires only first-order derivatives. We consider advection, mass-preserving transport, and incompressible flows as PDE models; variational regularization of the control variable promotes diffeomorphic transport maps, which we verify numerically. With a line search safeguard, GA-NGMRES converges globally. Since its FP map need not be contractive, we extend a recent analysis of NGMRES for noncontractive iterations to the alternating scheme. We compare GA-NGMRES to this Sobolev gradient descent, Anderson acceleration, a limited-memory BFGS method in the same Hilbert space, and Gauss-Newton-Krylov methods on real-world and synthetic data. GA-NGMRES converges where the unaccelerated scheme does not and outperforms Anderson acceleration. On our problems, it does not, in general, outperform the (quasi-)Newton methods, but it closes much of the gap to them; which method is fastest depends on the preconditioner, the regularization parameter, the data, and the stopping tolerance. GA-NGMRES is a simple and robust option when moderately accurate solutions suffice.
comment: 34 pages, 3 figures, 14 tables
♻ ☆ Online Nonconvex Decision Making with Approximate Oracles
Rui Chen, Oktay Gunluk, Andrea Lodi, Guanyi Wang
We study online decision making with possibly nonconvex (for example, combinatorial or integer) local feasible sets and convex long-term constraints. At each period, a decision maker selects a local action to maximize cumulative reward while ensuring that the sequence of actions satisfies the global constraints in the long term. It is known that $O(\sqrt{T})$ long-term constraint violation and $O(\sqrt{T})$ reward regret are achievable if given access to a local optimization oracle that exactly solves optimization problems over each local feasible set. Instead of requiring exact optimization over each local feasible set, we assume access to an approximate local optimization oracle that permits optimization errors quantified by two parameters $(δ_+,δ_\times)$. We develop an approximate online dual mirror descent algorithm and show that its guarantees depend on a feasibility slack parameter $\underline d$, which measures the compatibility between local feasible sets and the long-term constraint. Under the standard random permutation model, when $δ_+=O(1)$, $δ_\times<\underline d$ and $\underline d-δ_\times=Ω(1)$, the algorithm achieves $O(\sqrt T)$ long-term constraint violation and reward regret up to $O\bigl(\sqrt T+δ_\times T\bigr)+δ_+ T$. We also show a matching limitation: when $δ_+=0$ and $δ_\times>\underline d$, no online algorithm relying on such approximate oracle outputs can guarantee sublinear long-term constraint violation in general.
♻ ☆ A Theory of Information Architecture for Networked Decisions: Freshness, Locality, and Coordination
Scott Moeller, Bhaskar Krishnamachari
A broader view of a network can help agents coordinate, but collecting that view takes time. When is a fresh local observation more useful than an older view of the whole network, and when should an agent look only partway across it? We study agents that repeatedly minimize a shared quadratic cost in an environment that evolves independently of their actions. An information architecture specifies what each agent observes and how old those observations are. Each agent uses a synchronized neighborhood snapshot, so extending its scope also ages the nearby readings used in the decision. We assume that the optimal action with complete information is affine in the state, and that the conditional mean of the current state equals the old state scaled by a common exponential decay factor. Using the classical Marschak--Radner decomposition, we derive the delay threshold beyond which fresh local information outperforms a complete but older global view. This comparison allows non-Gaussian states and nonlinear decision rules. We then determine how far an agent should look by balancing the benefit of additional observations against their greater age. In a Gaussian spatial model on a line, we derive the optimal observation radius: looking beyond the local node pays only when information travels more than twice the spatial correlation length in one coherence time. The preferred information architecture also depends on the decision being made. On a fixed 64-node ring, increasing only the reach of the decision weights from 0.7 to 6 hops shifts the optimal observation radius from one to five hops.
comment: 32 pages, 6 figures. Manuscript source and complete reproduction materials are available at https://github.com/ANRGUSC/TINA
♻ ☆ Kernel-based potential mean-field games with unbiased random Fourier $U$-statistics
Yumiharu Nakano
We study the subclass of potential mean-field games in which the running interaction cost and the terminal target cost are both expressed through reproducing-kernel maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) penalties, and develop a computational framework that exploits this kernel structure. Both costs are estimated from finite-sample empirical distributions using a random Fourier U-statistic representation that is unbiased and has linear cost in the batch size. The drift of the controlled diffusion is parametrized by a neural network and trained via stochastic gradient descent. For population near-minimizers we prove convergence to the terminal-constrained problem as the penalty diverges, and show that the same limit is recovered almost surely when such controls are evaluated on independent finite samples under explicit coupling conditions on the penalty, random-feature count and sample size. The framework includes the kernel-MMD-penalty Schr{ö}dinger bridge problem as the special case of a vanishing interaction cost. Numerical experiments illustrate the method on the Schr{ö}dinger bridge problem in dimensions up to one hundred, and on an electric vehicle charging coordination problem with per-vehicle physical heterogeneity, where a control-dependent aggregate-demand cost produces a trade-off between peak normalized charging power and the terminal service level.
♻ ☆ DREAM: Delay-Resistant Acceleration with Momentum
Mert Gürbüzbalaban, M. Hamza Rafi, Necdet Serhat Aybat, Waheed U. Bajwa
With exact, delay-free gradients, Nesterov's accelerated gradient (NAG) achieves optimal $\sqrtκ$ dependence for $L$-smooth, $μ$-strongly convex objectives, where $κ=L/μ$; heavy-ball (HB) achieves the same scaling on strongly convex quadratics. In asynchronous and distributed settings, gradients can be inexact, with delays varying across workers and iterations. We isolate staleness using a fixed delay $τ\ge1$, replacing $\nabla f(y_k)$ with $\nabla f(y_{k-τ})$ at iteration $k$. Arjevani, Shamir, and Srebro establish a worst-case lower bound of $Ω(τ\sqrtκ\log(1/\varepsilon))$ iterations to reach objective error at most $\varepsilon$ as $\varepsilon\to0$. We show that for any fixed positive delay, neither NAG nor HB retains $\sqrtκ$-acceleration on strongly convex quadratics when updating every iteration, for any stable constant step size and positive momentum. We introduce delay-resistant accelerated momentum (DREAM), which decouples gradient-query extrapolation from momentum and uses explicit delay-dependent parameters. DREAM attains a linear convergence rate $1-Θ(1/(τ\sqrtκ))$ for all smooth strongly convex objectives as $κ\to\infty$, yielding complexity matching the delayed first-order lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Our proof combines characteristic-polynomial stability analysis on quadratics with an analytic Zames--Falb integral quadratic constraint certificate. We extend DREAM to smooth convex objectives, obtaining near-optimal iteration complexity up to logarithmic factors for sufficiently small target accuracy. Experiments on strongly convex quadratics and regularized logistic regression corroborate DREAM's accelerated condition-number dependence under delay, unlike NAG and HB, and suggest this scaling persists when parameters use a conservative bound on the true delay.
